title: Transformation or tumor heterogeneity: Mutations in EGFR, SOX2, TP53, and RB1 persist in the histological rapid conversion from lung adenocarcinoma to small‐cell lung cancer
author: Lidan Hao; Haiyang Chen; Lili Wang; Hanqiong Zhou; Zhe Zhang; Jing Han; Jiabao Hou; Yichen Zhu; He Zhang; Qiming Wang
text:
Abstract
The transformation from non‐small‐cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to small‐cell lung cancer (SCLC) is one of the mechanisms of epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR‐TKIs) resistance. Previous studies exhibited that the median transformation time was 17.8 months for NSCLC to SCLC. Here we introduced a case of lung adenocarcinoma (LADC) with EGFR19 exon deletion mutation in which the pathological transformation emerged only 1 month after lung cancer surgery and receiving EGFR‐TKI inhibitor. Eventually, the pathological examination confirmed the patient experienced a transformation from LADC to SCLC with EGFR, tumor protein p53 (TP53), RB transcriptional corepressor 1 (RB1), and SRY‐box transcription factor 2 (SOX2) mutation. Although the transformation of LADC with EGFR‐mutant into SCLC after targeted therapy was frequent, the pathological results of most patients were only biopsy specimens, which cannot rule out the existence of mixed pathological components of the primary tumor. In this case, the patient's postoperative pathology was sufficient to exclude the probability of mixed tumor components, confirming that the patient's pathological change was indeed transformation from LADC to SCLC. In addition, primary drug resistance in such a short time after surgery and osimertinib‐targeted therapy has not been reported before. We detected the molecular state of this patient before and after SCLC transformation through targeted gene capture and high‐throughput sequencing, and also found for the first time that the mutations of EGFR, TP53, RB1, and SOX2 continue to exist before and after transformation, but the mutation abundance is different. In our paper, the occurrence of small‐cell transformation is affected largely by these gene mutations.
Keywords: EGFR mutation, histological transformation, lung adenocarcinoma, small cell lung cancer, SOX2 mutation
A case of rapid small‐cell lung cancer transformation after receiving osimertinib after surgery, which was accompanied by mutations in EGFR, TP53, RB1, and SOX2.
INTRODUCTION
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutation is the most common mutation in lung adenocarcinoma (LADC), and its incidence varies significantly, ranging from 10% to 15% in Europe and the United States and 40% to 50% in Asia. 1 , 2 Of the patients who failed to receive epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR‐TKI) therapy, up to 10% of tumors exhibited transformation to small‐cell lung cancer (SCLC). 2 There are two hypotheses about this transformation. One is that SCLC cells trans‐differentiate from the primary adenocarcinoma during EGFR‐TKIs treatment, the other is that SCLC cells originate from pre‐existing SCLC cells and become dominant under the selection pressure of EGFR‐TKIs. In fact, most lung cancers are diagnosed by biopsy samples for pathological detection. Such samples are limited to fully display the pathological type of the tumor. When anticancer therapy suppresses the adenocarcinoma component in the tumor, the small‐cell carcinoma component becomes the main part of the tumor. 3 The pathological characteristics and molecular features of these transformed tumors have similar features to classical SCLC, such as loss of RB1 and TP53 activity. 2 Present studies support the biallelic inactivation of TP53 and RB1 as essential tumor suppressors in SCLC. 4 In addition, SOX2 is involved in the phenotypic transition between mesenchymal morphology and epithelial states of lung cancer cells, which can produce tumor heterogeneity. 5 Transformation or tumor heterogeneity is difficult to determine when LADC conversion SCLC in previous cases. However, in this report there were sufficient pathological samples to confirm the diagnosis of LADC, excluding mixed components. EGFR mutations are consistently present in LADC before transformation and SCLC after transformation, combined with the results of histopathology and molecular pathology. Both support the demonstration of tumor transformation rather than the conversion of intratumoral heterogeneity. Cancer stem cells (CSCs) affect tumor metastasis, recurrence, drug resistance, and cell differentiation. 6 As a stemness factor, SOX2 participates in the development of CSCs, 7 which is likely to influence SCLC transformation.
CASE PRESENTATION
The patient was a 65‐year‐old male with no history of smoking. Chest computed tomography (CT) showed right lung cancer on June 10, 2021 (Figure 1a). Hence, he underwent right lung cancer resection surgery but due to the limited conditions of local county hospitals, the lymph nodes were not cleaned. Postoperative pathology revealed poorly differentiated LADC with massive necrosis (solid adenocarcinoma, acinar adenocarcinoma, and micropapillary adenocarcinoma), vascular and nerve invasion positive, pleural involvement, and spread through air spaces positive (Figure 2a–d). The results of targeted gene capture and high‐throughput sequencing through the Illumina platform and Nextseq 550 showed EGFR Exon 19del p.Leu747‐Lys754delinsSerArgGlu(c.2240‐2260delinsCAAGAC) mutation, RB1 exon 11 P370fs p.Pro370fs(c.1109del) mutation, TP53 exon 7 R248Q p.Ary248Gln(c.743G>A) mutation, AKT serine/threonine kinase 1 (AKT1) exon 4 E17K p.Glu17Lys(c.49G>A) mutation, and SOX2 p.A267T(c.799G>A) mutation in abundances of 45.62%, 44.29%, 45.34%, 25.66%, and 29.42%, respectively (Table 1). The patient accepted pemetrexed plus carboplatin for one cycle after the surgery and withdrawal chemotherapy due to severe high fever, diarrhea, and other adverse reactions. The patient received osimertinib 80 mg per day on July 28, 2021 (Figure 1b). Unfortunately, he returned to our hospital with a cough and facial swelling in September 2021. Chest CT showed multiple enlarged metastasis lymph nodes in the right supraclavicular, mediastinum, and right hilum, and emboli formation in the superior vena cava. Head magnetic resonance imaging revealed a left frontal metastasis lobe nodule (Figure 1c,e). Color Doppler ultrasound revealed thrombosis in the left superficial femoral vein, popliteal vein, posterior tibial vein, anterior tibial vein, and part of the intermuscular vein of the calf.

The patient's tumor progressed rapidly, and the clinical manifestations and imaging features were inconsistent with the oncological features of LADC. The tumor marker neuron specific enolase (NSE) was 37.15 ug/L. Hence, we performed a second puncture to confirm the diagnosis. Finally, the right supraclavicular lymph node was punctured, and pathology and immunohistochemistry revealed neuroendocrine carcinoma infiltration and metastasis, tending to small‐cell carcinoma. Immunohistochemical results presented CK (+), CK7 (individual +), CD56 (focus +), CgA (partial +), Vimentin (−), TTF‐1 (+), Napsin A (−), SyN (+), P40 (−), Ki‐67 (80%+), and LCA (lymphocytes +) (Figure 2e–m). Lymph node tissue next‐generation sequencing showed EGFR Exon 19del p.Leu747‐Lys754delinsSerArgGlu(c.2240‐2260delinsCAAGAC) mutation, RB1 exon 11 P370fs p.Pro370fs(c.1109del) mutation, TP53 exon 7 R248Q p.Ary248Gln(c.743G>A) mutation, AKT1 exon 4 E17K p.Glu17Lys(c.49G>A) mutation, and SOX2 p.A267T (c.799G>A) mutation in abundances of 27.44%, 53.19%, 57.81%, 40.34%, and 31.95%, respectively (Table 1). The pathological results showed the patient had pathological transformation of LADC to SCLC, so he received etoposide plus carboplatin in combination with anlotinib concurrently for a massive tumor burden that obvious compression of the superior vena cava. On January 24, 2022, the patient received precise sequential radiotherapy to the chest (radiotherapy dose DT 60Gy/30f). During the treatment period, the patient underwent regular reexamination of chest CT and NSE, and the disease status reached partial remission (Figure 1d,f,g).
DISCUSSION
Lung cancer is one of the most usually diagnosed cancers and the prominent cause of cancer‐related deaths worldwide. The proportion of non‐small‐cell lung cancer (NSCLC) can reach about 85%. 1 Of note, among the patients with NSCLC, 3–15% will convert to SCLC. 3 , 8 In this case, the patient was diagnosed with LADC and underwent pulmonary resection, subsequently accepting the treatment of osimertinib. However, the clinical symptoms rapidly aggravated just after 1 month, and we performed a puncture examination and conformed to the diagnosis of SCLC. Clinically, the majority of advanced lung cancer diagnoses depend on tissue samples obtained by puncture, which often engenders insufficient tissue samples, incomplete test results, and easy omission of mixed components contained in tumor tissue. In this paper, no tumor component of SCLC was detected in the resection of lung cancer, and NSE was normal before surgery. Therefore, we deemed there was sufficient surgical tissue sample to support the initial diagnosis, excluding the possibility of tumor heterogeneity of the coexistence of LADC and SCLC components. Furthermore, the transformed SCLC still maintained the original EGFR mutation. Taken together, we tend to consider that the SCLC of this patient was not a mixed tumor or secondary primary tumor but a directly evolved result from the original LADC, 3 , 9 thereby ruling out the tumor heterogeneity hypothesis of small cell transformation. 10 Moreover, this is the first report of primary drug resistance with rapid small‐cell transformation from LADC after oral administration of third‐generation EGFR‐TKI (osimertinib) after surgery.
The pathological transformation from LADC to SCLC may be related to the common origin of CSCs. NSCLC and SCLC cells may originate from a common tumor stem cell. 11 During cell differentiation, alveolar type II cells can serve as cells of origin for adenocarcinoma cells. 3 , 12 The main origin cells of SCLC are neuroendocrine, which can be transformed from some alveolar type II cells after Tp53 and Rb1 deletion. 3 , 13 Hence, the transformation of LADC to SCLC may be a clonal evolution under the pressure of TP53 and Rb1 deletion, resulting in epigenetic changes and ultimately pathological transformation. 8 , 13 , 14
Excepting EGFR, TP53, and RB1 mutations before and after transformation, the patient also had mutations in SOX2. The abundance reduced in EGFR mutations and increased in TP53, RB1, and SOX2 after SCLC transformation, which is more in line with the molecular status of SCLC. 2 , 4 , 8 The study of George et al. indicated that TP53 and RB1 are essential tumor suppressors for SCLC, and LADC with the complete inactivation of both RB1 and TP53 is predisposed to transform into SCLC. 14 Some studies have proved that the overexpression of RB1 leads to the inhibition of SOX2, 15 and TP53 also promotes the differentiation of human embryonic stem cells by inhibiting SOX2 and other factors. 16 SOX2 can promote the expression of EGFR through positive feedback in lung cancer. 5 These gene mutations may play a crucial role in small‐cell transformation in this report.
SOX2 is a transcription factor that regulates the CSCs, which can maintain the undifferentiated cells and promote the malignant development of tumors. 5 CSCs have higher tumorigenesis properties, and the transcriptional factor SOX2 plays a vital role in maintaining the unique properties of CSCs. 17 Studies have shown that the interaction between SOX2 and transforming growth factor β affects the TKI tolerance of lung cancer with EGFR and the phenotypic transition between the mesenchymal and epithelial state of lung cancer, which can produce tumor heterogeneity. 5 In this case, it may be the critical factor that promotes the transformation from lung cancer to SCLC. TKI treatment favored the selection of lung cancer cells displaying mesenchymal morphology with deficient SOX2 expression, whereas SOX2 expression suppressed TKI tolerance and inhibited the mesenchymal phenotype of lung cancer cells with EGFR mutation. 5 Therefore, the deficiency of SOX2 accelerates the TKI resistance and promotes phenotypic transformation. Studies revealed that the overexpression of SOX2 can be detected in 71% of neuroendocrine tumors, but it is frequently detected in 10–50% of adenocarcinomas. 18 In this case, the abundance of SOX2 mutation increased after SCLC transformation, which is consistent with this study.
The transformation time affects patient survival to a large extent. Studies have shown that the median transformation time of LADC to SCLC was 17.8 months. 19 After surgery and treatment with osimertinib, the patient rapidly developed primary drug resistance, with the transformation time far below the reported median. We consider the potential cause of the rapid development of primary drug resistance in this case. First, NSCLC with EGFR‐mutant is more prone to undergo small cell transformation than EGFR wild type. 3 EGFR always exists before and after transformation, which may accelerate the process of SCLC transformation. Second, some studies demonstrated that EGFR‐TKI treatment induces the expression of CSCs marker, which leads the expression of SOX2 to upregulate. 20 SOX2, as a tumor stem factor, influences EGFR‐TKI drug resistance and tumor phenotypic transformation in lung cancer. 5 In this paper, the mutation of SOX2 may promote the occurrence of SCLC transformation to a certain extent. Finally, LADC with complete inactivation of Rb1 and TP53 were 43‐fold (relative risk 42.8, 95% CI 5.88–311) more likely to transform to SCLC during treatment. 14 As mentioned above, the disease transformation developed rapidly from LADC to SCLC.
In this study, the transformation time was shorter, and the clinical symptoms were severe when the transformation occurred, which is more different than an ordinary transformation in clinical practice. Although the tumors after transformation retained the original EGFR mutation, the expression was significantly reduced, suggesting that these tumors were no longer driven by EGFR signaling and that EGFR‐mutated SCLC maintained resistance to EGFR‐TKI and patients benefited limited from EGFR‐TKIs. 2 , 8 , 9 We adopted a strict standard radiotherapy and chemotherapy regimen for SCLC and combined it with antivascular drugs to relieve the symptoms of superior vena cava compression, and the patient's condition quickly achieved partial remission. We observed the molecular state before and after transformation through targeted gene capture and high‐throughput sequencing. Mutations in EGFR, TP53, RB1, and SOX2 persist from the initial diagnosis to transformation. The mutation of SOX2 is a potential mechanism to influence CSCs. Consequently, targeting SOX2 may be a promising therapeutic strategy to control small‐cell transformation. This is the first report of primary drug resistance in LADC with EGFR mutation associated with CSCs and stemness factors. It is also the first to describe the mutation state before and after SCLC transformation at the gene level. The interplay between EGFR, TP53, Rb1, and Sox2 jointly promoted and accelerated the process of small cell transformation in this case report. High‐throughput sequencing can detect and predict the occurrence and prognosis of tumors earlier.
